Round scad Decapterus punctatus is a small, schooling carangid widely distributed across the western Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico. Field surveys conducted off the southeastern United States have documented that individuals attain a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size limits reported for this species across its geographic range. Comparisons with congeneric taxa, such as Decapterus macarellus, indicate that Round scad reaches a somewhat smaller ultimate length, a distinction likely linked to differences in foraging ecology and habitat use. The size at which sexual maturation occurs has been estimated from histological examination of gonadal tissue in specimens collected during spring spawning aggregations. Puberty in this species is reached when individuals achieve a total length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to approximately the first year of life under typical thermal regimes. This relatively modest size at maturity is characteristic of many small pelagic carangids and is thought to reflect an adaptive trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth.

The reproductive biology of Decapterus punctatus has been characterized through analysis of oocyte size-frequency distributions and batch fecundity estimates from gravid females captured in the Gulf of Mexico. Under water temperatures of 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C], females release approximately 137,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 137,000 eggs per spawning event] on average over the course of the spawning season, spawning multiple times per season [F_R_i = multiple times per season]. This figure integrates both the number of eggs released per spawning event and the frequency of those events, reflecting the high fecundity characteristic of pelagic spawners that produce numerous buoyant, planktonic eggs. Spawning activity in Round scad is protracted, typically extending from late spring through early autumn, with peak reproductive effort coinciding with periods of elevated primary productivity. The strategy of producing large numbers of small, yolk-poor eggs is common among carangids and offsets relatively low per-offspring investment against high early-life mortality in the planktonic environment.

Detailed observations of early life stages in Decapterus punctatus have provided insights into the energetic constraints facing newly hatched larvae. The dry weight at birth, corresponding to the mass of the yolk-sac larva immediately following eclosion, is approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], a value derived from the species' egg diameter of roughly one millimeter. This minute starting mass imposes a narrow window for the onset of exogenous feeding, given that endogenous yolk reserves are rapidly depleted during the first few days of life. Larvae must successfully transition to feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton within a critical period to avoid starvation. Experimental rearing trials conducted at a stable temperature of 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C] indicate that the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilization to hatching, is approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] under those conditions. This incubation period aligns well with predictions based on the temperature-dependent developmental rates of other tropical and subtropical carangids and is notably shorter than the incubation times observed in cooler-water congeners.

As Round scad progresses through its larval and juvenile stages, substantial gains in body mass are observed prior to the onset of reproductive activity. The wet weight at puberty, determined from individuals collected at the length of sexual maturation, averages 15 grams [Wwp = 15 grams], a mass that represents a considerable increase over the natal dry weight and reflects the intensive feeding and growth that occur during the planktivorous post-settlement phase. Young-of-the-year juveniles recruit to coastal nursery habitats such as seagrass beds and nearshore reef edges, where they feed on small crustaceans and fish larvae. Growth during this period is rapid, and by the end of the first year, many individuals have already reached the size threshold for sexual maturation. The ultimate wet weight of fully grown adult Round scad has been assessed from length-weight relationships derived from extensive fishery-independent survey data, with the largest recorded individuals attaining a maximum wet weight of 300 grams [Wwi = 300 grams]. This upper mass limit distinguishes Decapterus punctatus from its larger-bodied congener Decapterus tabl and is consistent with its ecological role as a mid-level planktivore in pelagic food webs.

Longevity estimates for Decapterus punctatus have been derived from analysis of otolith microincrements in specimens collected across its range. Under the thermal conditions prevalent in subtropical waters, where annual mean temperatures approach 24.3 °C [T = 24.3 °C], the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small, fast-growing carangids and stands in contrast to the decadal longevities observed in larger, slower-growing members of the family such as Seriola dumerili. The relationship between temperature and metabolic rate likely governs this pace of life, with elevated environmental temperatures accelerating physiological processes and compressing the organismal lifespan. Annual mortality rates are correspondingly high, and the population is sustained through high fecundity and early maturation rather than extended individual survival. Tagging studies have further revealed that Round scad undertakes seasonal migrations along the continental shelf, moving inshore during warmer months for spawning and feeding before retreating to deeper waters in winter, a migratory pattern that influences both growth rates and vulnerability to commercial fisheries.
